title: New Zealand Races to Vaccinate Endangered Birds as Deadly H5N1 Reaches Its Shores
excerpt: The country is rushing to protect 300 breeding pairs of five critically endangered species after confirming its first cases of the lethal bird flu strain.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • New Zealand confirmed its first H5N1 cases in two birds last week.
  • The country is vaccinating 300 breeding pairs of five endangered bird species.
  • Poultry producers are moving hens indoors to prevent outbreaks.
  • Oceania was the last region free of H5N1 until recently.
  • H5N1 has devastated global poultry populations, leading to mass culls.
  • New Zealand confirmed its first cases of H5N1 avian influenza in two native birds, raising alarms for its unique wildlife.
  • The country is vaccinating 300 breeding pairs of five critically endangered bird species, including the kākāpō, to combat the virus.
  • The kākāpō population is particularly vulnerable, with only 235 individuals remaining on a single island sanctuary.
  • H5N1 has previously devastated bird populations globally, with poultry being the most affected species in terms of numbers.

Last Refuge Falls

No country is more devoted to its birds than New Zealand. Bird song marks 7 a.m. on public radio, the people call themselves Kiwis, and each year the nation holds a popular vote to crown its Bird of the Year.

So when officials confirmed last week that two birds had tested positive for the deadly H5N1 strain of avian influenza — a brown skua at Wellington's Petone Beach on July 15 and a native swamp harrier in Wairarapa two days later — the news landed hard.

H5N1 has carved a destructive path across the globe since first establishing itself in Europe in 2020, killing hundreds of millions of birds and infecting mammals from foxes to polar bears. Oceania had been the last major region free of the strain until an infected seabird was found on a Western Australian beach in June.

"These birds are only found in New Zealand; they're not found anywhere else in the world, so it's important to us," biosecurity minister Andrew Hoggard said.

A Vaccination First

In a step few countries have attempted, New Zealand is rushing to vaccinate 300 breeding pairs of five critically endangered native species. The kākāpō — a flightless, nocturnal parrot found nowhere else on Earth — is at the top of the list.

Bird flu poses an acute risk to the kākāpō because most of the surviving population, just 235 birds, lives on a single tiny island sanctuary off the coast of Rakiura/Stewart Island, surrounded by seabirds that could carry the virus.

"There are a lot of seabirds coming in there that the kākāpō might interact with, and that's a higher risk for that particular species," Ash Murray, biosecurity manager at New Zealand's conservation department, told CNN.

"Some species might not notice it at all, and some will die in large numbers."

— Mary van Andel, New Zealand's chief veterinary officer

The Poultry Threat

Native birds are not the only concern. Globally, the humble chicken has been the species most devastated by H5N1 in sheer numbers. When poultry are infected, survival rates are near zero, leading governments worldwide to slaughter entire flocks. In the United States alone, at least 174 million chickens have been culled.

The Poultry Crisis Looms
›174 million chickens culled in the U.S. due to H5N1.
›New Zealand's poultry exports suspended after H7N6 outbreak.
›Grocers warn against panic-buying eggs and chicken.
›Free-range hens moved indoors to mitigate risk.

Hoggard warned New Zealand would follow a similar path if a widespread poultry outbreak occurs, which could leave eggs and chicken in short supply on supermarket shelves. Grocers have already begun warning consumers not to panic-buy. Some poultry producers have proactively moved free-range hens indoors.

New Zealand had its first brush with avian influenza in late 2024 when a different strain, H7N6, was detected at a commercial poultry farm in Otago. About 200,000 chickens at Mainland Poultry's Hillgrove Farm were destroyed, and all poultry exports were temporarily suspended.

Marine Mammals at Risk

At the Ōamaru penguin colony in the South Island, where tourists watch hundreds of little blue penguins waddle ashore at sunset, visitors are now asked to disinfect their shoes on arrival. The country's oldest zoo has cancelled close-encounter experiences with penguins.

Officials are also watching New Zealand's marine mammals. In June, scientists revealed that H5N1 had wiped out an estimated 13,000 seal pups — three-quarters of the population — on the subantarctic Heard and McDonald Islands near Australia. New Zealand has more than 200,000 fur seals but fewer than 5,000 mature New Zealand sea lions.

"It is significantly rarer," Murray said of the sea lion. "So, we're keeping a close eye on that species."

Preparing for the Long Fight

Marine Mammals Under Threat
›H5N1 wiped out 13,000 seal pups on Heard and McDonald Islands.
›New Zealand has over 200,000 fur seals.
›Fewer than 5,000 mature New Zealand sea lions.
›Visitors disinfect shoes at Ōamaru penguin colony.

Being the last major landmass to face H5N1 has given New Zealand years to prepare. The Ministry for Primary Industries, the Department of Conservation, the Ministry of Health, and Health New Zealand have been working with industry and local councils to ready response plans.

"It's here forever," Murray said. "It will be about helping our species best adapt to that new threat."
